issues.description: The manuscript states that 40 participants entered the experiment after training exclusions, and then states that the high-confidence exclusion criterion 'resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded).' However, 40 − 23 = 17 excluded, not 5. Alternatively, 40 − 5 = 35 included, not 23. The parenthetical claim of 5 exclusions is irreconcilable with the inclusion count of 23.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the set size conditions.

issues.description: The Experiment 1 Procedure section states participants used a 2-point confidence scale (1 = guess, 2 = certain), whereas the Figure 1 caption describes a 4-point scale (1 = guess, 4 = certainty). This is a direct contradiction that affects interpretation of what constitutes a 'high confidence' trial and the comparability of Experiment 1 to Experiments 2–4.
issues.quote: indicated their confidence by clicking on one of two boxes (from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain) [Procedure]... Subsequently she indicated confidence in her judgment (1 = guess, 4 = certainty) [Figure 1 caption]

issues.description: For the Experiment 2 follow-up ANOVA on non-illusory errors, the text states 'only Memory Delay was a relevant factor (BFm = 42)... BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay' and that Target Type was irrelevant. However, Table 4 shows Memory Delay BFincl = 0.064 (evidence AGAINST inclusion) and Target Type BFincl = 39,110.895 (strong evidence FOR inclusion). These values are directly opposite to what the text describes, suggesting row labels or values are swapped, which undermines the interpretation of non-illusory error patterns in Experiment 2.
issues.quote: For other, non-illusory errors only Memory Delay was a relevant factor (BFm = 42... Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay) but this increase was the same for pseudo- and real letter targets

issues.subcategory: forced error due to response display design
issues.description: In Experiment 1, on half of pseudo-letter target trials, the pseudo-letter itself was absent from the response display while its real counterpart was present. Participants who correctly remembered the pseudo-letter were effectively forced to either select the real counterpart (inflating 'pseudo-to-real illusions') or choose 'none of these.' This design confounds genuine memory illusions with forced-choice artifacts. Although Experiments 2–4 address this by always including both target and counterpart, the Experiment 1 results are compromised by this design flaw.
issues.quote: If the target was a pseudo-letter, then it appeared as a response option randomly on half of those trials while on the other half of pseudo-letter trials only the real counterpart was one of the response options.

issues.description: The primary dependent variable is error rates on 'high confidence' trials, yet the manuscript never defines the threshold for classifying a trial as 'high confidence.' For the 4-point confidence scale used in Experiments 2–4 (and possibly Experiment 1), it is unclear whether 'high confidence' means confidence = 4, ≥ 3, or some other criterion. This is critical for replicability and interpretation.
issues.quote: focusing on high confidence errors: errors where the participant explicitly indicates to know the answer, and has not just guessed

issues.description: Exclusion rates based on the high-confidence trial criterion are very high: at least 17 of 40 participants (42.5%) in Experiment 1, 92 of 290 (31.7%) in Experiment 2, 5 of 64 (7.8%) in Experiment 3, and 4 of 95 (4.2%) in Experiment 4. The severe exclusion in Experiments 1 and 2 raises serious concerns about selection bias, as included participants differ systematically from excluded participants in their confidence profiles (e.g., Experiment 1: 53.8% vs. 26.2% high-confidence rate). No analysis of whether excluded participants differ on other characteristics is provided.
issues.quote: Included participants had on average 53.8% high confidence trials over all critical conditions (range: 36.3 – 93.2, sd: 13.9). Excluded participants had on average 26.2% high confidence trials over all conditions (range 3.6 – 47.7%, sd: 13.0).

issues.subcategory: alternative explanation for temporal increase inadequately addressed
issues.description: The core argument that illusions are memory-based (not perceptual) rests on their increase over time. However, an equally plausible alternative is that at shorter delays, residual sensory information helps participants override a pre-existing response bias toward real letters, and as this sensory trace degrades, the response bias dominates. This does not require any active transformation of memory content. The authors' dismissal of response bias ('the pattern of responses across conditions is consistent with memory-driven processes rather than response bias') is not backed by any formal analysis or modeling.
issues.quote: if the illusions arose completely during perception, they ought not to increase over time... This effect must be due to processes ongoing in STM: Had these illusory memories been the result of changes in perception, they should have been present at the earlier probe as well.

issues.description: The asymmetry between pseudo-to-real and real-to-pseudo errors could reflect a simple response bias toward selecting familiar stimuli (real letters) rather than a genuine memory illusion. This is especially concerning given that in Experiments 1–2, real letters were more prevalent as targets, but even in Experiments 3–4 with balanced sets, familiarity-based response bias would still predict more pseudo-to-real selections. The authors dismiss response bias in one sentence without formal testing (e.g., signal detection modeling or drift-diffusion modeling that could separate bias from sensitivity).
issues.quote: However, this is unlikely because the pattern of responses across conditions is consistent with memory-driven processes rather than response bias.

issues.subcategory: confidence scales differ across experiments without comparison
issues.description: Experiment 1 uses either a 2-point or 4-point confidence scale (contradictory reports), while Experiments 2–4 use a 4-point scale. The comparability of 'high confidence' responses across experiments is never discussed, despite the fact that the proportion of trials classified as high confidence varies substantially (e.g., ~54% in Experiment 1 vs. ~49% in Experiment 2 vs. ~39% in Experiment 3). This undermines cross-experiment comparisons.
issues.quote: indicated their confidence by clicking on one of two boxes (from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain) [Exp 1]... indicated her confidence (on a scale from 1 - 4) [Exp 2]

issues.description: The Experiment 4 results section refers to 'Figure 5' for its error rate data, but Figure 5 is already assigned to Experiment 3. The correct reference should be Figure 6, which is the caption label used for the Experiment 4 figure.
issues.quote: Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials.

issues.description: In Experiment 4, the text states there was 'a smaller increase in illusory errors from short to long delays when the target was mirrored (5% difference) compared to when the target was a real letter (4% difference).' However, 5% > 4%, so the mirrored (pseudo-letter) target condition actually had a LARGER increase, not smaller. The comparison is stated in the wrong direction.
issues.quote: There was a smaller increase in illusory errors from short to long delays when the target was mirrored (5% difference) compared to when the target was a real letter (4% difference).

issues.description: For real-letter targets in Experiment 1, the text states the target appeared as a response option on 83% of trials and its pseudo-letter counterpart appeared on 16% of trials, summing to 99% rather than 100%. While likely a rounding issue, it leaves ambiguity about the remaining 1% of trials.
issues.quote: it appeared as a response option on a randomly selected 83% of the trials, while its mirror reversed (pseudo-letter) version appeared as a response option on the other 16% of the trials

issues.description: No pre-registration is mentioned for any of the four experiments. Given the multiple analytic choices (exclusion criteria, confidence thresholds, model selection strategy, follow-up tests, whether to collapse across conditions), the absence of pre-registration introduces substantial researcher degrees of freedom.

issues.subcategory: different and unjustified stopping rules across experiments
issues.description: Experiments 3 and 4 used sequential Bayesian stopping rules but with different BF thresholds (BF ≥ 6 for Experiment 3, BF ≥ 10 for Experiment 4). No justification is given for either threshold or for why they differ. Optional stopping with Bayesian methods is acceptable in principle, but the choice of threshold still affects the sample size and potentially the results.
issues.quote: once the outcome crossed a BF of 6, testing would stop [Exp 3]... once the outcome crossed a BF of 10, testing would stop [Exp 4]

issues.description: None of the four experiments report effect sizes (e.g., Cohen's d, eta-squared, or posterior parameter estimates) for any comparison. Only Bayes Factors are reported. Without effect sizes, the practical magnitude of the observed illusion effects cannot be assessed and meta-analytic integration is hindered.

The manuscript only reports error rates (illusory and other) without reporting correct response (hit) rates across conditions. Hit rates would contextualize the error rates, allow assessment of overall task difficulty, and help rule out floor/ceiling effects.

issues.subcategory: weak manipulation check for expectation cue
issues.description: In Experiment 2, the color cue manipulation was checked only via a post-experiment questionnaire that asked what the experiment was about. The null finding for cue color could simply mean participants never learned the cue-probability contingency, rather than that 'transiently induced expectations' cannot affect memory. No trial-by-trial or block-by-block learning analysis was conducted, and no objective measure of contingency awareness was obtained.
issues.quote: Participants filled out a brief questionnaire in which they were invited to indicate what the experiment was about after the experiment. The relationship between the colour of the cue and the nature of the target was not mentioned in any of the responses.

issues.description: Experiment 4 was conducted online via Zoom/Neurotask on participants' own laptops, introducing variability in display characteristics (size, resolution, luminance, viewing distance, timing precision) that could affect stimulus perception and memory. No calibration was performed and no comparison to lab-based findings is discussed, yet results are directly compared to Experiments 1–3.
issues.quote: the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting. Participants that signed up to take part in the experiment were invited to join a Zoom meeting at a preset time.

issues.description: The construct 'world knowledge' is operationalized exclusively through familiarity with letter orientation. The only attempt to test a broader notion of expectation (cue color in Experiment 2) failed. Yet the paper makes broad claims about 'world knowledge' and 'prior expectations' shaping STM. The generalizability of this single operationalization to the broader construct is limited.
issues.quote: world knowledge: prior expectations about the likely events or objects, based on lifelong learning and development. In this case, the relevant expectations relate to a highly overlearned category of visual symbols, namely letters of the alphabet.

issues.description: The General Discussion claims that 'all stages of STM are susceptible to illusory memories' but then immediately acknowledges the experiments do not test iconic memory. The claim of 'all stages' is overstated given that one of the three proposed stages was not tested.
issues.quote: The fact that all stages of STM are susceptible to illusory memories has important implications for vision research... Our experiments currently do not test whether illusory memories arise in IM

issues.description: The General Discussion states illusory memories increase 'from 0.5 s to 3 s' but Experiment 1's short delay was 0.75 s (not 0.5 s). Only Experiment 4 used a 0.5 s short delay. This misrepresents the time course tested across experiments.
issues.quote: Experiments 1, 2 and 4 show that illusory memories make up a larger part of high confidence responses as time passes (from 0.5 s to 3 s).

issues.description: Experiment 1 included two set sizes (6 and 8 letters) but all analyses average across set sizes. No set-size-specific results are reported, and the potential influence of memory load on illusion rates is not examined despite being a theoretically relevant variable.
issues.quote: when the results were averaged across the set size conditions

issues.description: Different letters, when mirrored, may differ in their visual discriminability from their real counterparts (e.g., mirrored 'J' vs. mirrored 'R'). No analysis of letter-specific illusion rates is provided, which would help disambiguate the 'world knowledge' explanation from a visual similarity account at a finer grain.

issues.subcategory: fuzzy trace theory dismissal is oversimplified
issues.description: The authors argue FTT cannot explain the findings because FTT predicts that high similarity between target and lure facilitates false memories, which they claim is inconsistent with their data showing abundant false memories despite high similarity. However, this argument is confused: abundant false memories for highly similar lures is exactly what FTT would predict. The authors seem to misinterpret FTT's prediction as being that high similarity should reduce false memories, when in fact FTT would predict more false memories when gist overlap is high.
issues.quote: FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should facilitate false memories. This is not consistent with the current data: The mirrored counterpart (the real letter) and the target (the pseudo-letter) are extremely similar, yet false memories are abundant.

issues.description: Experiment 1 included an extensive training phase with a 75% accuracy exclusion criterion, while Experiments 2–4 only had brief practice trials. This introduces systematic differences in participant selection and preparation across experiments that could affect the magnitude of observed illusions, yet cross-experiment comparisons are made throughout.
issues.quote: Participants could only participate in the actual experiment, if they scored higher than 75% correct (averaged across all trials) on the final 10 blocks of training.

issues.subcategory: no analysis of excluded vs included participants
issues.description: Given the high exclusion rates (especially Experiments 1 and 2), no comparison of demographic or performance characteristics between included and excluded participants is provided beyond average confidence rates. The systematic exclusion of less-confident participants could introduce selection bias if confidence and susceptibility to illusions are correlated.

Multiple follow-up ANOVAs and t-tests are conducted after the main Bayesian ANOVA (e.g., separate ANOVAs for illusory vs. non-illusory errors in Experiment 2, follow-up t-tests in Experiment 4). These follow-up tests do not appear to be corrected for multiplicity, and the choice of which follow-ups to conduct appears data-driven.
issues.quote: Follow-up ANOVAs conducted separately for each error type showed that for illusory errors, the optimal model consisted of the factors Memory delay, Target type and the interaction between the two

issues.description: As memory fades, participants' criteria for what qualifies as a confident response may shift. At longer delays, participants may lower their threshold for reporting 'high confidence,' which could disproportionately admit error trials into the high-confidence category. This criterion shift could account for the increase in high-confidence illusions over time without any actual memory transformation occurring.
issues.quote: as the quality of the memory representation decreases through decay or interference, world knowledge plays an increasingly large role within STM
